# R8.5 acceleration benchmark (GENERATED by tools/bench/benchmark_r85.py)

**Verdict: HARD_STOP_TRANSFER_DOMINATED.** Under the current link, every representative workload spends longer moving data over SPI than the FPGA spends computing, and the FPGA path is slower than the F133 CPU even with the worst-case CPU assumption. This is the change order's HARD STOP condition (5.3). It holds for the T35 too, since the link and the no-FPGA-to-BT820 rule are the same. The bottleneck is the architecture, not the FPGA part.

Evidence: CPU = dynamic instruction counts from an RV64IM ISS (checksums equal to a native run) × assumed CPI 1–2 at an assumed 1.0 GHz. Link = the real F133 driver code against the board model at SCK 10 MHz, 2 µs per CS transaction. FPGA = RTL perf counter for the transform; the other workloads are planning estimates with no RTL. No hardware measurement.

Link fit (driver + model): 0.790 µs per byte effective, 88 µs per batch, 72.9 SPI bytes per transform job.

Link scenarios:
* A_current_SPI_10MHz (RTL mailbox limit sys/8; modelled with the real driver)
* B_SPI_50MHz_single (needs a new source-synchronous mailbox slave; ASSUMPTION)
* C_QSPI_4x50MHz (needs 3 more FPGA pins + new slave + F133 SPI0 quad host mode; ASSUMPTION)

CPU instructions per item (ISS): transform 351.4, collision 18.2, particles 24.0, fir 236.1.

## What this means

* Data has to come back over SPI, because the F133 alone commands the BT820 (protected baseline; no FPGA→BT820 path). So offload pays only when CPU work per byte moved exceeds about (f_cpu / link bandwidth) cycles: ≈ 900 cycles/byte at today's ≈ 1.1 MB/s effective. The ARC-1 2D workloads need about 5–60 CPU instructions per byte moved.
* With the multiplier mapping (8 of 72 MULT18X18D), 87 MHz timing and the PSRAM interface, the ECP5 meets every logic gate. It does not meet the CO 5.3 success criterion.
* Options for the owner (CO 8.2: report, do not silently change): see STATUS_R85.md 'Stop/revert options'.
